First, we rewrite the integral as

$$
\int (1-9z)^{-1/2}\,\text{d}z.
$$

Now, we let $u=1-9z.$ Then differentiating with respect to $z$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}z}=-9\,⟹\,\text{d}z=-\frac{1}{9}\text{d}u.
$$

We now write our integral in terms of $u,$ calculate the integral as normal, and write the final answer in terms of $u$ at the very end:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (1-9z)^{-1/2}\,\text{d}z & =\int {u}^{-1/2}\cdot (-\frac{1}{9}\text{d}u) \\  & =-\frac{1}{9}\int {u}^{-1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{9}\frac{1}{(1/2)}{u}^{1/2}+C \\  & =-\frac{2}{9}{u}^{1/2}+C \\  & =-\frac{2}{9}(1-9z)^{1/2}+C \\  & =-\frac{2}{9}\sqrt{1-9z}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Let's double-check that our result is correct. If we differentiate the result, then it should come out to the original integrand:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}z}[-\frac{2}{9}\sqrt{1-9z}+C] & =-\frac{2}{9}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}z}[\sqrt{1-9z}]+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}z}(C) \\  & =-\frac{2}{9}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}z}[(1-9z)^{1/2}]+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}z}(C) \\  & =-\frac{2}{9}\cdot \frac{1}{2}(1-9z)^{-1/2}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}z}(1-9z)+0 \\  & =-\frac{1}{9}\cdot (1-9z)^{-1/2}\cdot (-9) \\  & =(1-9z)^{-1/2} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-9z}}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$
